ideas.title: Copilot Critical Lens
ideas.summary: A browser-based playground that presents the same programming problem with three AI-generated solutions side-by-side, each annotated with a 'what could go wrong' callout; students vote on the best solution and see a live class-wide tally, training critical evaluation of AI code instead of blind acceptance.
ideas.description: The instructor pastes a short programming prompt (e.g., 'write a function that returns the second-largest element in a list') and clicks Generate. The app calls the Claude API three times with slightly varied temperatures and system prompts to produce three distinct solutions, each placed in a syntax-highlighted code panel. Alongside each panel, Claude generates a 2-3 bullet 'risk annotation': edge cases the code mishandles, readability issues, off-by-one risks, or assumptions baked into the implementation. Students (joined via a shareable URL, no login required) read the three solutions and their annotations, then cast a single vote for which they consider most trustworthy. A live bar chart below updates in real time via Supabase subscriptions so the class sees the vote distribution form. After the instructor closes voting, a reveal panel shows the 'instructor verdict' explaining what actually matters most in this specific case and why naive trust in any one AI output is risky. Sessions are ephemeral by default; instructors can optionally save a session to a Supabase-backed library for reuse in future classes. A dozen seed prompts (sorting, recursion, string parsing, pointer arithmetic) are bundled so the tool is immediately usable without any prompt authoring.
keyFeatures: One-click generation of three stylistically distinct AI solutions from a single prompt, using varied temperatures and system-prompt framing
Per-solution 'risk annotation' panel generated by Claude: edge cases, readability gaps, hidden assumptions, and failure scenarios
Anonymous real-time voting with live bar chart updated via Supabase subscriptions, shareable via URL with no student login
Instructor reveal panel explaining the authoritative verdict and what critical evaluation of AI code means in context
Bundled seed prompt library (sorting, recursion, string parsing, pointer arithmetic) for immediate classroom use
ideas.techStack: React + Vite + Tailwind, Claude API (claude-haiku-4-5 for speed, sonnet for annotations), Supabase (Postgres + real-time subscriptions) for voting state
ideas.whyInteresting: Repeated ITiCSE and SIGCSE findings show students treat AI-generated code as authoritative rather than as a starting point for critical review. This tool makes the evaluation skill explicit and social: seeing classmates disagree on which solution is best prompts students to articulate their own reasoning. The weekend scope is achievable because the core interaction is simple (generate, annotate, vote, reveal) and the real-time voting state is trivially handled by Supabase subscriptions.
ideas.inspiredBy: ITiCSE 2025 work on fostering responsible AI use through negative expertise, and growing HN discussion threads about the danger of AI-generated code being accepted without review in educational settings

ideas.title: Social SOS Board
ideas.summary: A real-time classroom board where students post brief 'stuck' moments by topic and assignment; peers can +1 the same struggle, and the instructor sees a live heatmap of which concepts are blocking the most students right now, counteracting the AI-routing of help-seeking that erodes peer learning communities.
ideas.description: Students open a course URL and see a grid of concept tiles (e.g., 'pointer arithmetic', 'recursion base case', 'merge sort invariant') pre-configured by the instructor. Clicking a tile opens a short form: describe your stuck moment in one sentence, optionally add a code snippet (under 200 characters), and choose whether to post anonymously or with your name. The post appears immediately on the board under that concept tile. Other students can click a +1 button on any post that describes the same confusion they have, or leave a 'I figured it out' reply that marks the thread resolved. The instructor dashboard shows three live panels: a heatmap grid of concept vs. time (updated every 30 seconds via Supabase subscriptions) so they see which topics are spiking right now; a 'trending stuck' feed of the most +1'd open threads in the last 15 minutes; and a resolution rate panel showing what percentage of threads got a peer answer before requiring instructor intervention. The goal is to make peer help-seeking the path of least resistance: posting to the board is faster than opening ChatGPT, and seeing that six classmates have the same confusion normalizes struggling and invites peer response. Instructors can pin a concept tile to trigger a 'live intervention' banner, signaling they are about to address it in class. At the end of each session, the board archives to a JSON export instructors can paste into their course retrospective notes.
keyFeatures: Concept-tile grid pre-configured by the instructor; students click a tile to post a one-sentence stuck moment with optional anonymous posting
+1 voting so students signal shared confusion without posting duplicates; 'I figured it out' reply marks threads resolved
Live heatmap grid (concept vs. time, 30-second refresh via Supabase subscriptions) showing which topics are spiking right now
Trending-stuck feed: the most +1'd open threads in the last 15 minutes, surfaced to the instructor in real time
Live intervention banner: instructor can pin a concept tile to signal 'addressing this now in class'
ideas.techStack: React + Vite + Tailwind, Supabase (Postgres + real-time subscriptions), Recharts for the heatmap and trend charts, no custom backend beyond Supabase row-level security for anonymous posts
ideas.whyInteresting: Recent ITiCSE 2025 research showed that AI chatbot availability significantly reduces the rate at which students seek help from peers or instructors, degrading the social learning infrastructure of the course. This tool does not fight AI adoption; it makes peer help-seeking marginally easier than opening ChatGPT by reducing the activation energy to 'click a tile, type a sentence.' The real-time heatmap turns the instructor's gut sense of 'the class seems confused about X' into a live signal they can act on mid-lecture.
ideas.inspiredBy: ITiCSE 2025 findings on how AI chatbot adoption routes help-seeking away from peers and instructors, reducing the formation of peer learning communities in CS courses

ideas.title: Natural Language Decomposer
ideas.summary: Students build a web IDE feature in which they describe each programming subtask in plain English; an LLM converts each description into a callable function stub with typed signature and docstring; the student implements each stub; a visualization panel plays back the decomposition steps as a dependency graph, making the planning process visible and assessable.
ideas.description: This three-week assignment asks students to build a tool that externalizes the problem-decomposition stage of programming, the step that distinguishes experienced programmers from beginners but is typically invisible to instructors. In week one students implement the prompt-to-stub pipeline: the user types a sentence describing a subtask ('given a list of integers, return the k largest values in descending order'), clicks 'Generate Stub', and the app calls the Claude API to produce a Python or JavaScript function stub with a typed signature, a docstring restating the intent, and a TODO comment body. The generated stub is inserted into an editable code panel below. Students can generate as many stubs as they need before writing any implementation code. Week two focuses on the visualization: each stub generation event is logged with a timestamp and the natural language description; after the student clicks 'Finalize Decomposition', the app renders a dependency graph (using a simple DAG layout) where each node is a function stub and directed edges are drawn when one stub's description references another stub's name or concept. Week three is implementation and reflection: students fill in the stub bodies in the code panel, run a provided test harness, and then record a 5-minute screencast explaining their decomposition choices, what they would change in hindsight, and whether the tool helped or hindered their thinking. Instructors receive the full decomposition log (which stubs were generated, in what order, with what descriptions, and how many iterations each took) alongside the final code, giving them visibility into a part of the programming process that normal code submission hides entirely.
keyFeatures: Natural language to typed function stub pipeline: one-sentence description generates a stub with typed signature, docstring, and TODO body via Claude API
Iterative stub refinement: students can regenerate or manually edit any stub before committing to the decomposition
Dependency graph visualization: auto-layout DAG where nodes are stubs and edges are inferred from inter-stub references in the descriptions
Decomposition log: every stub generation event (timestamp, NL description, generated stub, iteration count) recorded and exportable for instructor review
Screencast reflection deliverable: students record a 5-minute video explaining decomposition choices and what they would change, submitted alongside the code
ideas.techStack: React + Vite + Tailwind + Monaco Editor for code panel, Claude API (claude-sonnet-5 for stub generation), Flask + SQLite for decomposition log persistence, Dagre.js for DAG layout rendering
ideas.whyInteresting: Research in CS education consistently identifies problem decomposition as a critical bottleneck for novice programmers, yet it is almost never explicitly taught or assessed because it is invisible in the submitted artifact. This assignment makes the planning process a first-class deliverable. The LLM acts as a scaffolding partner rather than a code generator: it handles the boilerplate of stub formalization so the student can focus on the intellectual work of identifying subtasks and their dependencies. The dependency graph visualization gives students an external representation of their own thinking that is often surprising and educational in itself.
ideas.inspiredBy: SIGCSE TS 2026 findings that describing programming functionality in natural language may improve decomposition quality in novice programmers, and HN posts about coding agents that compile intent into deterministic DAGs of subtasks

ideas.title: Skill-Adaptive Misconception Feedback: Calibrating LLM Explanation Depth to Student Proficiency in CS1
ideas.summary: Extends an ITiCSE 2025 finding that high- and low-skill students need fundamentally different feedback depth for the same misconception by building a pipeline that infers a student's skill tier from Jolly Feedback submission patterns and generates tier-calibrated LLM explanations, then measures whether matched feedback reduces resubmission cycles relative to one-size-fits-all output.
ideas.description: A 2025 ITiCSE paper surveyed introductory programming students about their perceptions of misconception indicators and found that low-skill students were overwhelmed by rich explanatory feedback while high-skill students found minimal 'indicator-only' feedback insufficiently actionable. Both groups received the same misconception label but needed different depths of elaboration to act on it effectively. Current automated feedback systems, including Jolly Feedback, emit the same error messages and test-case output regardless of student proficiency. This research proposes a three-phase study using retrospective Jolly Feedback logs from UW CSS 142. Phase one establishes a skill-tier classifier: using submission metadata already in the Jolly Feedback database (time-to-first-pass, total attempt count across the assignment, error-message diversity across attempts, and fraction of tests passed on first submission), train a lightweight classifier that assigns each student-assignment pair to one of three skill tiers (emerging, developing, proficient) without using any self-reported data or prior grade information. The classifier uses features that are observable in real time during active submission, making it applicable to live deployment. Phase two designs and validates the tiered feedback templates: for each tier, Claude API is prompted to generate explanations at matched depths (tier 1: one-sentence misconception label only; tier 2: label plus a concrete counter-example showing correct behavior; tier 3: label plus Socratic question sequence guiding the student to identify their own error). A panel of three CS instructors rates 60 generated explanations (20 per tier) on appropriateness for the target skill level using a 5-point rubric. Phase three deploys the full pipeline in a pilot CSS 142 assignment: the skill classifier assigns a tier at the moment of submission, the appropriate LLM explanation is appended to the standard Jolly Feedback test-case output, and the primary outcome is whether students who received matched-depth feedback required fewer subsequent submissions to pass the assignment compared to a matched historical control group from the prior quarter.

papers.title: How Do Learners With Varying Skills Perceive Misconception Indicators and Feedback?
papers.abstract: This paper reports a survey study of introductory programming students examining how learners at different skill levels perceive misconception indicators and associated feedback. High-skill students found minimal indicator-only feedback insufficiently actionable, while low-skill students were overwhelmed by rich explanatory feedback. Both groups received the same misconception label but had fundamentally different informational needs, suggesting that adaptive feedback depth calibrated to proficiency level could improve feedback utility across the skill distribution.
papers.relevance: Directly motivates the research question: if different skill tiers need different feedback depths for the same misconception, a system that infers skill tier from observable submission patterns and generates tier-matched LLM explanations may outperform Jolly Feedback's current one-size-fits-all output. The survey methodology also provides a validated rubric for the instructor-panel rating phase in phase two.

additionalRefs.title: A Systematic Literature Review of Automated Feedback Generation for Programming Exercises
additionalRefs.authors: Hieke Keuning, Johan Jeuring, Bastiaan Heeren
additionalRefs.relevance: Comprehensive survey of 101 automated feedback tools, classifying feedback types and their pedagogical effectiveness. Provides the definitional framework for feedback depth levels (indicator, elaborated, Socratic) used in the tier template design and situates the proposed system within the broader automated feedback literature.

additionalRefs.title: The Relative Effectiveness of Human Tutoring, Intelligent Tutoring Systems, and Other Tutoring Systems
additionalRefs.relevance: Establishes that the effectiveness of tutoring interventions is strongly modulated by the learner's skill level and the granularity of the hint or feedback provided, supporting the core hypothesis that one-size-fits-all automated feedback underperforms matched adaptive feedback across proficiency levels.

additionalRefs.title: Adaptive Feedback Strategies in Intelligent Tutoring Systems: A Review
additionalRefs.relevance: Reviews adaptive feedback strategies in ITS research, including skill-level detection and differential feedback delivery. Provides the state-of-the-art baseline against which the proposed Jolly Feedback extension can be compared and motivates the use of submission metadata rather than standardized tests for tier classification.

researchPlan.overview: This research tests whether a lightweight, submission-metadata-based skill-tier classifier can route CS1 students to depth-appropriate LLM-generated misconception explanations, reducing resubmission cycles compared to Jolly Feedback's current uniform output. The study proceeds in three phases: retrospective classifier construction, expert validation of tiered feedback templates, and a prospective pilot in one CSS 142 assignment.

milestones.goal: Feature engineering and skill-tier classifier construction
milestones.deliverable: Anonymized export of CSS 142 Jolly Feedback submission logs (2+ quarters); feature set defined (time-to-first-pass, attempt count, error-message diversity, first-submission test-pass fraction); skill-tier labels assigned retrospectively using end-of-quarter grade quartiles as ground truth; logistic regression and random forest classifiers trained and cross-validated; F1 scores reported per tier

milestones.goal: Tiered feedback template design and LLM pipeline implementation
milestones.deliverable: Three prompt templates per tier (indicator-only, label plus counter-example, label plus Socratic sequence) implemented as Claude API calls; pipeline accepts a (submission diff, error category, skill tier) tuple and returns a formatted feedback string; 60 generated explanations (20 per tier) produced for expert rating

milestones.goal: Expert panel rating and template refinement
milestones.deliverable: Three CS instructors rate 60 generated explanations on a 5-point appropriateness rubric (blind to tier assignment); inter-rater reliability computed (Krippendorff alpha); template prompts revised based on patterns in low-rated outputs; final pipeline version frozen for pilot deployment

milestones.goal: IRB submission and Jolly Feedback pilot integration
milestones.deliverable: IRB protocol submitted for prospective pilot (historical control design requires no prospective student consent beyond standard course participation notice); skill-tier classifier and LLM feedback pipeline integrated into Jolly Feedback development branch; one CSS 142 assignment identified for pilot with historical control cohort from the prior quarter

milestones.goal: Pilot deployment and primary data collection
milestones.deliverable: Pilot assignment live with matched-depth LLM feedback appended to standard Jolly Feedback output; submission counts, time-to-pass, and error sequences logged for treatment cohort; historical control data extracted from prior-quarter logs for the same assignment

Statistical comparison of treatment vs. historical control on resubmission count and time-to-pass (Mann-Whitney U, effect size d); subgroup analysis by skill tier to test whether matched feedback helps most in the emerging tier; full paper draft targeting SIGCSE TS, ICER, or AIED

researchPlan.resources: Anonymized Jolly Feedback submission logs from CSS 142 (2+ quarters for classifier training and historical control); Claude API (Haiku tier for batch pilot delivery, Sonnet for template development); three CS instructor volunteers for expert rating panel; IRB for prospective pilot component; TA support during pilot assignment week.

risks.risk: End-of-quarter grade quartiles used as skill-tier ground truth may not align with within-assignment proficiency, inflating classifier performance estimates
risks.mitigation: Cross-validate classifier against an alternative ground truth (first-assignment pass rate as a proxy for prior preparation) and report both F1 scores; if agreement is low, use a two-label tier system (emerging vs. proficient) rather than three to reduce boundary ambiguity

risks.risk: Historical control comparison may be confounded by year-over-year changes in course content, student population, or assignment difficulty
risks.mitigation: Select an assignment that has been unchanged for at least two prior quarters; control for assignment difficulty by normalizing resubmission counts against the class median for each quarter; report the raw difference and the normalized effect separately

risks.risk: Low-skill students may find even the Socratic (tier 1) feedback overwhelming if the misconception itself is deeply entrenched, producing null or negative effects in the emerging-skill group
risks.mitigation: Pre-register the subgroup analysis plan before pilot deployment to avoid post-hoc adjustment; if the emerging-tier effect is null or negative, treat this as a finding motivating a four-tier model with a 'foundational' tier that offers human escalation rather than automated elaboration
